units.title: Model notation
units.objective: Interpret conditional model notation and parameters
units.explanation: In $p(y \mid x, \theta)$ the bar reads 'given'. The model receives the input $x$ (for example, review text) and uses its learned parameters $\theta$ (weights and bias) to assign a probability to the label $y$. In binary classification $p$ abbreviates $p(y=1 \mid x, \theta)$, so class 0 has probability $1-p$. A probability is not a label: a decision rule such as 'predict 1 if $p \ge 0.5$' converts it into a class.
units.workedExample: A model outputs $p = 0.7$ for the review 'Great battery life'. It assigns 0.7 to the positive label and 0.3 to the negative label. With a 0.5 threshold it predicts label 1. The value 0.7 itself is the model's confidence, not the label.

skills.objective: Interpret conditional model notation and parameters

units.title: Dataset likelihood
units.objective: Construct likelihood under the stated independence assumption
units.explanation: The likelihood $L(\theta)$ is the probability the model assigns to the observed labels. If labels are conditionally independent given their inputs and $\theta$, it factorises: $L(\theta) = \prod_i p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta)$. The labels are fixed data; fitting changes $\theta$, which changes every factor. Independence is an assumption, not a guarantee about the data.
units.workedExample: Three examples receive true-label probabilities 0.9, 0.6 and 0.5. Assuming conditional independence, $L(\theta) = 0.9 \times 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.27$. A different $\theta$ would give different probabilities and a different likelihood.

skills.objective: Construct likelihood under the stated independence assumption

units.title: Log objective
units.objective: Connect likelihood, log likelihood and negative log likelihood
units.explanation: Because $\log$ is strictly increasing on positive values, $L$ and $\log L$ have the same maximisers. The log also turns the product into a sum: $\log L = \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta)$. Negating turns maximisation into minimisation, so maximising $L$ is equivalent to minimising the negative log likelihood. Dividing by the fixed dataset size $n$ (a mean) rescales without moving the minimiser.
units.workedExample: With true-label probabilities 0.9 and 0.5: $\log L = \ln 0.9 + \ln 0.5 \approx -0.105 - 0.693 = -0.798$. Summed NLL is 0.798 and mean NLL is 0.399; both are minimised by the same $\theta$.

skills.objective: Connect likelihood, log likelihood and negative log likelihood

units.title: Meaning of binary cross-entropy
units.objective: Explain what BCE measures and distinguish it from accuracy
units.explanation: Binary cross-entropy penalises a model for assigning low probability to the true label. Since $-\log q$ grows without bound as $q \to 0$, a confident wrong prediction gets a large loss. BCE scores probabilities, not just whether the thresholded class is correct, so equal accuracy does not imply equal BCE. A low BCE does not certify calibration.
units.workedExample: For true label 1, model A predicts 0.95 and model B predicts 0.55. Both are correct at a 0.5 threshold, but A's loss is $-\ln 0.95 \approx 0.051$ while B's is $-\ln 0.55 \approx 0.598$.

skills.objective: Explain what BCE measures and distinguish it from accuracy

units.title: Calculation and application
units.objective: Calculate BCE and use aggregate losses to compare predictions
units.explanation: $\mathrm{BCE}(y,p) = -[\,y \log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\,]$ with natural logs and $p \in (0,1)$. For $y=1$ only $-\log p$ remains; for $y=0$ only $-\log(1-p)$ remains. The loss is never negative. To compare models on the same examples, average each model's per-example losses and prefer the lower mean.
units.workedExample: For $y=0$ and $p=0.4$: $\mathrm{BCE} = -\ln(1-0.4) = -\ln 0.6 \approx 0.511$. The class-1 probability 0.4 must be converted to the true-label probability 0.6 before taking the log.

skills.objective: Calculate BCE and use aggregate losses to compare predictions

units.title: Derivation
units.objective: Derive BCE from the Bernoulli likelihood
units.explanation: A Bernoulli label has probability $p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$, which equals $p$ when $y=1$ and $1-p$ when $y=0$. Taking $-\log$, the log of a product becomes a sum and each exponent comes down: $-[\,y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\,]$. Summed over examples this is the dataset NLL. Two-class one-hot cross-entropy with $t=(1-y,y)$ and probabilities $(1-p,p)$ reduces to the same expression.
units.workedExample: For $y=0$: $-[\,0\cdot\log p + 1\cdot\log(1-p)\,] = -\log(1-p)$, matching the class-0 branch of BCE.

skills.objective: Derive BCE from the Bernoulli likelihood
